# autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autocfg/

## Expand description

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[build-dependencies]
autocfg = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
fn main() {
    let ac = autocfg::new();
    ac.emit_has_type("i128");
    // (optional) We don't need to rerun for anything external.
    autocfg::rerun_path("build.rs");
}
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

[§](https://docs.rs#caution)Caution

Many of the probing methods of `AutoCfg` document the particular template they
use, **subject to change**. The inputs are not validated to make sure they are
semantically correct for their expected use, so it’s *possible* to escape and
inject something unintended. However, such abuse is unsupported and will not
be considered when making changes to the templates.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AutoCfg](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)
- Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg`output in build scripts.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A common error type for the `autocfg`crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit](https://docs.rs/fn.emit.html)
- Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)- possibility
- Indicates to rustc that a config flag should not generate an `unexpected_cfgs`warning
- [new](https://docs.rs/fn.new.html)
- Creates a new `AutoCfg`instance.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_env.html)- env
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var`changes.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_path.html)- path
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if `path`changes.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rsomics_average_degree_connectivity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rsomics-average-degree-connectivity/0.1.1/rsomics_average_degree_connectivity/

## Expand description

Average degree connectivity (Pastor-Satorras k_nn) — value-exact port of
`networkx.average_degree_connectivity`.

For an undirected unweighted graph, the average degree connectivity maps a
degree `k` to the average degree of the nearest neighbours of the nodes of
degree `k`. Following networkx, it is computed as the accumulation

```
dsum[k]  += sum(deg(w) for w in neighbours(v))      for every node v of degree k
dnorm[k] += deg(v)
result[k] = dsum[k] / dnorm[k]
```
A self-loop on `v` counts twice toward `deg(v)` (as in networkx), but `v`
appears exactly once in `neighbours(v)` — so it contributes `deg(v)` once to
its own dsum term. `dnorm[k] = k * count(k)`, so the k=0 class (isolated
nodes) would divide by zero; networkx returns `dsum[0]` verbatim there.
Edge-list input cannot introduce a degree-0 node, so that branch is
unreachable here.

Barrat, Barthélemy, Pastor-Satorras & Vespignani, “The architecture of complex weighted networks”, PNAS 101(11):3747-3752 (2004).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Average](https://docs.rs/struct.AverageDegreeConnectivity.html)- Degree - Connectivity
- Result payload: the `k -> value`map serialised as an object under`by_degree`.
- [Connectivity](https://docs.rs/struct.Connectivity.html)
- One `degree -> average neighbour degree`row, sorted by ascending degree.
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.Graph.html)
- Undirected simple graph over interned integer node ids.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_degree_connectivity.html)- degree_ - connectivity
- Compute the average degree connectivity, replicating networkx’s dsum/dnorm accumulation so the division structure — and thus the f64 result — matches value-exactly.
- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_degree_connectivity_from_edge_list.html)- degree_ - connectivity_ - from_ - edge_ - list
- Parse an edge list and compute the average degree connectivity in one call.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_edge_list.html)- edge_ - list
- Parse a whitespace-delimited `u v`edge list.`#`comments and blank lines are skipped. Parallel edges are deduplicated and self-loops kept once in the adjacency, matching the`nx.Graph`that`nx.parse_edgelist`builds. A kept self-loop appears a single time in`adj[v]`; its double contribution to`deg(v)`is added in`average_degree_connectivity`.

# durability - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/durability/0.6.12/durability/

## Expand description

`durability`: crash-consistent persistence primitives.

Scope:

- directory abstraction (`Directory`)
- on-disk framing constants (`formats`)
- append-only record log (`recordlog`)
- generic write-ahead log (`walog`)
- CRC-validated checkpoint snapshots (`checkpoint`)
- generic recovery (`recover::recover_with_wal`) and segment-specific recovery (`recover`,`publish`) with the default`postcard`feature

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `postcard`(default): serde/postcard typed WAL, checkpoint, recovery, and publish helpers.
- `async`: tokio-compatible async directory abstraction.
- `mmap`: mmap and advisory helpers.

With `default-features = false`, the crate still provides the directory abstraction,
raw record logs, raw checkpoint payloads, WAL framing/maintenance, and sync helpers.

[§](https://docs.rs#contract-what-you-can-rely-on)Contract (what you can rely on)

This crate is designed around two different “strength levels”:

- **Crash-consistent + integrity-checked**(default)- Detects corruption (CRC/magic/version/type mismatches) and errors loudly.
- Supports best-effort recovery of a **torn tail**(partial record write) in the**final**log segment.
- Guarantees a **prefix property**under best-effort replay: recovered operations are a prefix of the successfully written operation stream (no garbage / no reordering).

- **Stable-storage durability**(opt-in)- Requires explicit barriers (`fsync`/`sync_all`) and sometimes**parent directory sync**.
- Use `storage::sync_file``storage::sync_parent_dir``flush_and_sync()`helpers where you need “survives power loss after success” semantics.

- Requires explicit barriers (

Terminology:

- `flush()`is a- **visibility boundary**, not a stable-storage guarantee.
- “Best-effort” is intentionally narrow; it never masks corruption.

Note: this crate intentionally exposes *traits and framing*.
Higher-level crates generally decide directory layout, naming, and lifecycle policies,
but some primitives (notably `walog`) assume a conventional `wal/` directory.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use error::`- [PersistenceError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.PersistenceError.html);
- `pub use error::`- [PersistenceResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.PersistenceResult.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [Directory](https://docs.rs/storage/trait.Directory.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [FsDirectory](https://docs.rs/storage/struct.FsDirectory.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [MemoryDirectory](https://docs.rs/storage/struct.MemoryDirectory.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_dir/index.html)- dir
- Async directory trait and blocking adapter.
- [checkpoint](https://docs.rs/checkpoint/index.html)
- Generic checkpoint file (single snapshot blob).
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for `durability`.
- [mmap](https://docs.rs/mmap/index.html)
- Memory-mapped file access with advisory hints.
- [publish](https://docs.rs/publish/index.html)
- Crash-safe checkpoint publishing and WAL truncation helpers.
- [recordlog](https://docs.rs/recordlog/index.html)
- Append-only record log (generic WAL primitive).
- [recover](https://docs.rs/recover/index.html)
- Crash recovery using checkpoint + WAL replay.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- Storage abstraction for durability.
- [walog](https://docs.rs/walog/index.html)
- Write-ahead log (WAL) for incremental updates.

# rsomics_average_neighbor_degree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rsomics-average-neighbor-degree/0.1.1/rsomics_average_neighbor_degree/

## Expand description

Average neighbor degree — value-exact port of `networkx.average_neighbor_degree`.

For each node v: `sum(degree(w) for w in neighbors(v)) / degree(v)`.
Isolated nodes (degree 0) get 0.0.

Nodes are interned to integer indices for O(m) cache-friendly computation.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.Graph.html)
- Parsed graph: intern table + integer adjacency.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_neighbor_degree.html)- neighbor_ - degree
- Compute average neighbor degree for every node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_edgelist.html)- edgelist
- Parse an edge-list from text (whitespace-delimited `u v`lines). Lines starting with`#`and blank lines are skipped.

# rustld - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustld/0.1.56/rustld/

## Expand description

Rustld is a modern (and working) ELF x86_64 & aarch64 loader (static & dynamic linker + compatible glibc & musl) written in Rust
You can run (almost) **everything** with it.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-sdk)Rust SDK:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// With syscall trampoline obfuscation:
rustld::ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
// Without obfuscation:
rustld::ElfLoader::new().execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
// Optional explicit entrypoint:
rustld::ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes_with_entry(
    target_bytes, target_argv,
    Some("hello"), // or None
    None,          // or Some(0x399)
    None, None, false,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)Basic usage example:

```
use std::{ffi::OsStr, os::fd::AsRawFd, os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt};
use rustld::ElfLoader;
fn main() {
    unsafe {
        let argv_storage = collect_process_arguments();
        if argv_storage.len() < 2 {
            eprintln!(
                "Usage: rustld [--entry-symbol <name> | --entry-addr <addr>] <program> [args...]"
            );
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        let mut args = argv_storage.into_iter();
        let _self_name = args.next();
        let mut entry_symbol: Option<String> = None;
        let mut entry_address: Option<usize> = None;
        let mut target_argv: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
        while let Some(arg) = args.next() {
            if arg == "--entry-symbol" {
                let Some(symbol) = args.next() else {
                    eprintln!("Error: --entry-symbol expects a value");
                    std::process::exit(1);
                };
                entry_symbol = Some(symbol);
                continue;
            }
            if arg == "--entry-addr" {
                let Some(raw_addr) = args.next() else {
                    eprintln!("Error: --entry-addr expects a value");
                    std::process::exit(1);
                };
                let parsed = parse_address(&raw_addr);
                entry_address = Some(parsed);
                continue;
            }
            target_argv.push(arg);
            target_argv.extend(args);
            break;
        }
        if target_argv.is_empty() {
            eprintln!("Error: missing target program path");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        if entry_symbol.is_some() && entry_address.is_some() {
            eprintln!("Error: --entry-symbol and --entry-addr are mutually exclusive");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        let target_bytes = map_file_readonly(OsStr::from_bytes(target_argv[0].as_bytes()));
        #[cfg(debug_assertions)]
        eprintln!("Executing target binary: {}", target_argv[0]);
        if entry_symbol.is_some() || entry_address.is_some() {
            ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes_with_entry(
                target_bytes,
                target_argv,
                entry_symbol.as_deref(),
                entry_address,
                None,
                None,
                false,
            );
        } else {
            ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
        }
    }
}
fn parse_address(raw: &str) -> usize {
    let (digits, radix) = if let Some(hex) = raw.strip_prefix("0x") {
        (hex, 16)
    } else if let Some(hex) = raw.strip_prefix("0X") {
        (hex, 16)
    } else {
        (raw, 10)
    };
    match usize::from_str_radix(digits, radix) {
        Ok(value) => value,
        Err(_) => {
            eprintln!("Error: invalid entry address: {raw}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}
fn collect_process_arguments() -> Vec<String> {
    std::env::args_os()
        .map(|arg| arg.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
        .collect()
}
unsafe fn map_file_readonly(path: &OsStr) -> &'static [u8] {
    use rustld::syscall::mmap::{self, MAP_PRIVATE, PROT_READ};
    let file = match std::fs::File::open(path) {
        Ok(file) => file,
        Err(error) => {
            eprintln!("Error: could not open target binary: {error}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };
    let length = match file.metadata() {
        Ok(metadata) => metadata.len() as usize,
        Err(error) => {
            eprintln!("Error: could not stat target binary: {error}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };
    if length == 0 {
        eprintln!("Error: target binary is empty");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let mapped = mmap::mmap(
        core::ptr::null_mut(),
        length,
        PROT_READ,
        MAP_PRIVATE,
        file.as_raw_fd() as isize,
        0,
    );
    let mapped_addr = mapped as isize;
    if mapped_addr < 0 {
        eprintln!("Error: could not map target binary");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    core::mem::drop(file);
    core::slice::from_raw_parts(mapped as *const u8, length)
}
```

# posthog_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/posthog-rs/0.17.1/posthog_rs/

## Expand description

Official Rust SDK for PostHog.

Use [ client](https://docs.rs/fn.client.html) to construct a

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)

`Client`[to capture analytics events, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.evaluate_flags)

`Client::evaluate_flags`[for feature flag evaluation.](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluateFlagsOptions.html)

`EvaluateFlagsOptions`See the [PostHog Rust SDK documentation](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/rust)
for installation, configuration, and more examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `posthog-rs` to your `Cargo.toml`, then initialize a client with your
project API key.

```
use posthog_rs::{client, EvaluateFlagsOptions, Event};
#[cfg(feature = "async-client")]
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str()).await;
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog
        .evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())
        .await?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
#[cfg(not(feature = "async-client"))]
fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str());
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog.evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

# ferridriver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver/0.5.0/ferridriver/

## Expand description

ferridriver – Rust-based browser automation library.

Provides a Playwright-shaped API for browser automation across
multiple backends (CDP WebSocket, CDP Pipes, Playwright `WebKit`,
`WebDriver` `BiDi`).

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver::{chromium, Page};
use ferridriver::options::{LaunchOptions, RoleOptions};
let browser = chromium().launch(LaunchOptions::default()).await?;
let page = browser.new_page_with_url("https://example.com").await?;
// Playwright-style locators
page.get_by_role("link", &RoleOptions { name: Some("More".into()), ..Default::default() })
    .click(None).await?;
// Content extraction
let title = page.title().await?;
let md = page.markdown().await?;
```

- [web_](https://docs.rs/web_error/index.html)- error
- `WebError`— live handle for page-side unhandled errors and unhandled promise rejections.
- [web_](https://docs.rs/web_socket_route/index.html)- socket_ - route
- `WebSocketRoute`— page-side WebSocket interception (- `page.routeWebSocket`/- `context.routeWebSocket`, Playwright 1.60).

# sim_lib_music_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-music-core/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_music_core/

## Expand description

Core music model layer for the SIM music constellation.

SIM is a Rust runtime with multiple codec surfaces; this crate supplies the concrete music domain that those surfaces operate on. It defines the music object model (notes, chords, melodies, scores), the descriptor metadata that describes music components and their ports and parameters, events and lanes, the piano roll and time grid, players and playables, performances and takes, the arranger, freeze surfaces, traces, the component registry, and the citizen integration that registers these types with the runtime.

- Renders a music object into clipped, stably ordered note play events.
- [scales_](https://docs.rs/fn.scales_chords_player_descriptor.html)- chords_ - player_ - descriptor
- Returns the descriptor for the Scales and Chords player.
- [scales_](https://docs.rs/fn.scales_chords_player_id.html)- chords_ - player_ - id
- Returns the registry id of the scales-chords player.
- [stable_](https://docs.rs/fn.stable_event_order.html)- event_ - order
- Sorts events in place into a deterministic order.
- [stable_](https://docs.rs/fn.stable_lane_order.html)- lane_ - order
- Sorts lanes deterministically by order, then id, then kind.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_envelopes.html)- envelopes
- Drains a play stream into transport envelopes over a memory-local profile.
- [tempo_](https://docs.rs/fn.tempo_lfo_descriptor.html)- lfo_ - descriptor
- Returns the descriptor for the Tempo LFO modulator.
- [tick_](https://docs.rs/fn.tick_to_kernel_tick.html)- to_ - kernel_ - tick
- Encodes a tick on a named clock as a kernel `Tick`reference.
- [time_](https://docs.rs/fn.time_to_tick.html)- to_ - tick
- Converts a musical time in beats to ticks at the given pulses-per-quarter.

# wikrs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wikrs/0.1.0/wikrs/

## Expand description

**wikrs** — fast, honest wikitext extraction and parsing.

Turns MediaWiki wikitext (the markup inside Wikipedia XML dumps) into clean
plain text or a structured AST, and **emits a diagnostic when it hits input
it can’t faithfully handle instead of silently corrupting the output**.
Validated on the full English Wikipedia (7.19M articles, 98.0% of pages
convert with zero residual markup).

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
// Parse wikitext into an AST + diagnostics, then render plain text.
let parsed = wikrs::parser::parse("'''Earth''' is a [[Planet|planet]].");
assert!(parsed.diagnostics.is_empty());
assert_eq!(wikrs::render::plain(&parsed.nodes), "Earth is a planet.");
// Or the Stage 1 one-shot stripper (fast, lossy, no diagnostics).
assert_eq!(
    wikrs::extract::strip("'''Earth''' is a [[Planet|planet]]."),
    "Earth is a planet."
);
```
Reading a whole dump ([ dump::open](https://docs.rs/dump/fn.open.html), or

[for parallel bz2 decoding) yields](https://docs.rs/dump/fn.open_multistream.html)

`dump::open_multistream`[s whose](https://docs.rs/dump/struct.Page.html)

`dump::Page``text` feeds the same
two entry points. The `wikrs` CLI wraps exactly this pipeline.Pre-1.0: the API surface is the modules documented below; items marked
`#[doc(hidden)]` are internal plumbing with no stability promise.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- The wikitext AST (Stage 2).
- [diag](https://docs.rs/diag/index.html)
- Diagnostics (DESIGN.md §7). The engine’s honesty mechanism: when it meets a
construct outside the declared support range, it emits an `Unsupported`diagnostic with the original source span — instead of silently producing something plausible but wrong.
- [dump](https://docs.rs/dump/index.html)
- Streaming reader for Wikimedia XML dumps (`pages-articles-multistream.xml.bz2`).
- [extract](https://docs.rs/extract/index.html)
- Stage 1: lossy `wikitext -> plain text`extraction.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parser: wikitext → AST + diagnostics, over a deliberately small but honest
subset (paragraphs, headings, bold/italic, links, nested & definition lists,
refs/nowiki/comments, inline HTML formatting, preformatted). Inline templates
are dropped with a `W-TEMPLATE`warning (we don’t expand them — that would sacrifice the speed that is the whole point); tables and structural HTML become`Node::Unsupported`
- [render](https://docs.rs/render/index.html)
- Render an AST to output. Stage 2 starts with plain text — the same product
as Stage 1’s `extract::strip`, but driven by a real parse so it can preserve structure. Structured (JSONL) and HTML renderers come later.

# zif_tiff - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zif-tiff/0.2.0/zif_tiff/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#zif-tiff)zif-tiff

`zif-tiff` is a Rust library for reading and writing [ZIF](https://docs.rs/SPECIFICATION.md), a tiled, multi-resolution image format for very large zoomable images. ZIF is a constrained subset of `BigTIFF`: every ZIF file is a valid TIFF file, but most TIFF files are not valid ZIF files.

ZIF stores image metadata in a BigTIFF-compatible container and stores each tile as an independent JPEG or PNG byte stream. This makes it a good fit for local files, HTTP range requests, object storage, and interactive viewers that only need a small part of a huge image at a time.

The core crate is Sans-IO: it parses metadata, plans byte-range requests, exposes tile locations, and writes ZIF structures without choosing a filesystem, HTTP client, async runtime, or image decoder for you.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

- zero dependencies in the core library
- Sans-IO reader and writer
- efficient byte-range access for huge files
- no JPEG or PNG decoding in core
- ergonomic tile iteration for viewports and zoom levels
- default `std`IO adapters for files and any`Read + Seek`/`Write + Seek`object
- optional `tokio`filesystem and`http`IO adapters
- generic over any `tower_service::Service`for HTTP range requests
- writer updates that keep the file valid at every step

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Read a ZIF file and inspect its dimensions:

```
use zif_tiff::{sample_zif_bytes, std::RangeReader};
let zif = RangeReader::from(sample_zif_bytes()).read_zif()?;
println!("{} x {}, {} levels", zif.width(), zif.height(), zif.level_count());
```
Use the Sans-IO reader when you want explicit control over range requests, for example to fetch the encoded tiles intersecting a viewport:

```
use zif_tiff::{sample_zif_bytes, Chunk, ReadStatus, Reader, std::RangeReader};
let mut io = RangeReader::from(sample_zif_bytes());
let mut reader = Reader::new();
let mut chunk = Chunk::default();
while let ReadStatus::Need { req, .. } = reader.advance(chunk)? {
    chunk = io.fetch(req)?;
}
let zif = reader.into_zif()?;
for tile in zif.get_cropped_level_tiles(0, (0..20, 0..20))? {
    let encoded_tile = io.fetch(tile.req())?;
    println!("tile {:?}, {} bytes", tile.position(), encoded_tile.bytes().len());
}
```
The bytes returned for a tile are the original encoded JPEG or PNG stream. Decode them with the image library appropriate for your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

Default features, including synchronous filesystem helpers:

```
[dependencies]
zif-tiff = "..."
```
Core/no-std only:

```
[dependencies]
zif-tiff = { version = "...", default-features = false }
```
With Tokio filesystem helpers:

```
[dependencies]
zif-tiff = { version = "...", features = ["tokio"] }
```
With HTTP range request support (generic over `tower_service::Service`):

```
[dependencies]
zif-tiff = { version = "...", features = ["http"] }
```
With async filesystem and HTTP helpers:

```
[dependencies]
zif-tiff = { version = "...", features = ["tokio", "http"] }
```
Feature flags:

- `std`: standard-library filesystem readers and writers, enabled by default
- `tokio`: Tokio-based filesystem readers and writers
- `http`: HTTP range reader generic over any- `tower_service::Service`(works natively with- `reqwest::Client`,- `hyper`, etc.)

[§](https://docs.rs#what-zif-contains)What ZIF Contains

A ZIF file represents one logical image as a chain of image directories. In the common pyramid layout:

- level 0 is the full-resolution image
- level 1 is approximately half resolution
- level 2 is approximately quarter resolution
- later levels continue down the pyramid

Each level is split into tiles. Each tile is independently compressed and can be fetched by byte range without reading or decoding the rest of the file.

The reader exposes:

- image dimensions
- level dimensions
- tile size and tile grid
- codec and color model metadata
- byte ranges for encoded tiles
- optional metadata and annotation ranges

The reader does not expose decoded pixels.

[§](https://docs.rs#reading)Reading

For normal reads, use an IO adapter to get a `Zif` object directly.

```
use zif_tiff::{sample_zif_bytes, std::RangeReader};
let zif = RangeReader::from(sample_zif_bytes()).read_zif()?;
println!("dimensions: {:?}", zif.dimensions());
println!("codec: {:?}", zif.codec());
println!("color model: {:?}", zif.color_model());
```
The same helper works with any `Read + Seek` object:

```
let bytes = zif_tiff::sample_zif_bytes();
let cursor = std::io::Cursor::new(bytes);
let zif = zif_tiff::std::read_zif(cursor)?;
assert_eq!(zif.dimensions(), (40, 40));
```
Optional adapters provide equivalent helpers for async files and HTTP:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let zif = zif_tiff::tokio::read_zif(file).await?;
// HTTP: works with any tower Service
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let url: http::Uri = "https://example.com/slide.zif".parse()?;
let mut http = zif_tiff::http::HttpRangeReader::new(client, url);
let zif = http.read_zif().await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#iterating-tiles)Iterating Tiles

All tiles at a level:

```
let zif = zif_tiff::sample::zif();
for tile in zif.get_level_tiles(0)? {
    println!("tile {} at {:?} uses bytes {:?}", tile.index(), tile.position(), tile.bytes());
}
```
Tiles intersecting a viewport:

```
let zif = zif_tiff::sample::zif();
for tile in zif.get_cropped_level_tiles(0, (0..20, 0..20))? {
    println!("visible tile {:?}, size {:?}", tile.position(), tile.size());
}
```
Tile values are lightweight metadata objects:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl Tile {
    pub fn level(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn index(&self) -> u64;
    pub fn col(&self) -> u64;
    pub fn row(&self) -> u64;
    pub fn position(&self) -> (u64, u64);
    pub fn size(&self) -> (u64, u64);
    pub fn bytes(&self) -> std::ops::Range<u64>;
    pub fn req(&self) -> zif_tiff::Request;
    pub fn codec(&self) -> zif_tiff::Codec;
}
```
Use `tile.bytes()` when you only need the raw byte range. Use `tile.req()` when passing the request to an IO adapter.

[§](https://docs.rs#io-adapters)IO Adapters

The core API works with any backend that can fetch byte ranges and return `Chunk` values. The `std` adapter works with files and with any `Read + Seek` object:

```
use zif_tiff::{sample_zif_bytes, std::RangeReader};
let mut io = RangeReader::from(sample_zif_bytes());
let chunk = io.fetch(zif_tiff::Request::new(0..16)?)?;
assert_eq!(chunk.range(), 0..16);
```
Optional adapters cover common filesystem and HTTP cases:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let mut file_io = zif_tiff::std::FileRangeReader::open("slide.zif")?;
let mut tokio_io = zif_tiff::tokio::FileRangeReader::open("slide.zif").await?;
// HTTP: reqwest::Client works as a tower Service
let http_io = zif_tiff::http::HttpRangeReader::new(reqwest::Client::new(), "https://example.com/slide.zif".parse().unwrap());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#low-level-sans-io)Low-Level Sans-IO

Use the Sans-IO `Reader` directly when integrating with a custom storage layer or when you need exact control over range requests and response chunks. `advance` accepts any valid chunk, not only the exact range it requested. This is useful for HTTP servers that return a larger range than requested or return the whole file. `Chunk` ties a byte range to the bytes for that range and rejects incoherent range/length pairs.

Custom backends are straightforward because the reader only needs `Request` in and `Chunk` out.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
while let zif_tiff::ReadStatus::Need { req, .. } = reader.advance(chunk)? {
    let bytes = object_store.get_range(req.range()).await?;
    chunk = zif_tiff::Chunk::new(req.range(), bytes)?;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#writing)Writing

The writer emits write operations for the caller to apply. It does not own a file handle and does not choose an IO backend.

Create a one-level image:

```
use zif_tiff::std::RangeWriter;
let mut file = RangeWriter::from(Vec::new());
let mut writer = zif_tiff::Writer::new()
    .dimensions((100_000, 80_000))
    .tile_size((512, 512))?
    .codec(zif_tiff::Codec::Jpeg)
    .color_model(zif_tiff::ColorModel::YCbCr)
    .channels(3)?
    .build()?;
file.apply(writer.put_tile((0, 0), b"encoded-jpeg")?)?;
let bytes = file.into_inner().into_inner();
println!("wrote {} bytes", bytes.len());
```
Create a conformant pyramid automatically:

```
use zif_tiff::std::RangeWriter;
let mut file = RangeWriter::from(Vec::new());
let mut writer = zif_tiff::Writer::new()
    .dimensions((100_000, 80_000))
    .tile_size((512, 512))?
    .pyramid()
    .codec(zif_tiff::Codec::Jpeg)
    .color_model(zif_tiff::ColorModel::YCbCr)
    .channels(3)?
    .build()?;
file.apply(writer.put_tile_at_level(1, (3, 4), b"encoded-jpeg")?)?;
```
Use `.pyramid()` to build levels down to a single tile, or `.pyramid_to_1x1()` to continue until the final level is exactly 1 x 1 pixels.

Update dimensions and continue adding tiles:

```
use zif_tiff::std::RangeWriter;
let mut file = RangeWriter::from(Vec::new());
let mut writer = zif_tiff::Writer::new()
    .dimensions((100_000, 80_000))
    .tile_size((512, 512))?
    .codec(zif_tiff::Codec::Jpeg)
    .color_model(zif_tiff::ColorModel::YCbCr)
    .channels(3)?
    .build()?;
file.apply(writer.set_dimensions(0, (120_000, 90_000))?)?;
file.apply(writer.put_tile((12, 8), b"encoded-jpeg")?)?;
```
Writer updates use an append-first, pointer-last layout. Existing valid structures remain in place until replacement structures and tile bytes have been written. The final pointer update switches the file to the new valid layout.

This makes repetitive updates practical: adding or replacing a tile does not require rewriting existing tile payloads.

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error Handling

Core errors are separate from IO adapter errors. Malformed files, invalid coordinates, arithmetic overflow, unsupported features, and incoherent chunks are reported as typed `zif_tiff::Error` values.

```
fn handle(reader: &mut zif_tiff::Reader, chunk: zif_tiff::Chunk) -> zif_tiff::Result<()> {
    match reader.advance(chunk) {
        Ok(_) => Ok(()),
        Err(zif_tiff::Error::MalformedFile(msg)) => {
            eprintln!("rejecting malformed file: {msg}");
            Ok(())
        }
        Err(err) => Err(err),
    }
}
```
The reader rejects structural violations such as invalid header constants, unsorted directory entries, missing required tags, invalid tile dimensions, tile count mismatches, and overflowing byte ranges. Unknown tags are ignored unless they contradict required ZIF metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-compatibility)Format Compatibility

ZIF is `BigTIFF`-compatible at the container level. A ZIF file can often be opened by TIFF tools that support tiled `BigTIFF` with JPEG or PNG compression.

The format is intentionally narrower than general TIFF. ZIF requires little-endian byte order, 64-bit offsets, tiled image data, 8-bit grayscale or RGB pixels, and self-contained JPEG or PNG tiles for baseline files.

See [SPECIFICATION.md](https://docs.rs/SPECIFICATION.md) for the complete binary format.

[§](https://docs.rs#testing-and-validation)Testing And Validation

The crate is designed to be tested at the format boundary:

- parse hand-built fixtures and malformed files
- round-trip files through the writer and reader
- verify generated files with TIFF tooling where available
- decode extracted JPEG and PNG tiles in tests
- exercise fragmented, oversized, duplicate, and non-exact range responses
- check huge-image arithmetic and edge-tile clipping

External crates are appropriate in tests and optional IO adapters. They are not required by the core reader, writer, and metadata model.

# tatara_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-wasm/0.2.115/tatara_wasm/

## Expand description

`tatara-wasm` — multi-runtime WASI/WASM host for tatara guests.

Five runtimes, one trait, Cargo feature flags. Consumers pick the runtime per workload via the Lisp surface:

```
(defguest fast-fn   :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmtime …))
(defguest k8s-fn    :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmedge …))
(defguest embed-fn  :kind (:wasm :runtime :wamr   :features (:aot #t :no-std #t)))
```
The runtime axis is first-class — all five are shipped with
production-grade implementations in Phase H.3 (wasmtime) and
H.4 (the rest). See `docs/declarative-guests.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.1 stub.** The `WasmRuntime` enum + `WasmEngine` trait
land here now so `tatara-vm` can reference them. Runtime bodies
are empty until H.3/H.4.

The complete sandwich:

# autocfg 1.5.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autocfg/1.5.1

# autocfg

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

## Minimum Rust version policy

This crate's minimum supported `rustc` version is `1.0.0`.  Compatibility is
its entire reason for existence, so this crate will be extremely conservative
about raising this requirement.  If this is ever deemed necessary, it will be
treated as a major breaking change for semver purposes.

# autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autocfg/1.5.1/target-redirect/autocfg/

## Expand description

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[build-dependencies]
autocfg = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
fn main() {
    let ac = autocfg::new();
    ac.emit_has_type("i128");
    // (optional) We don't need to rerun for anything external.
    autocfg::rerun_path("build.rs");
}
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

[§](https://docs.rs#caution)Caution

Many of the probing methods of `AutoCfg` document the particular template they
use, **subject to change**. The inputs are not validated to make sure they are
semantically correct for their expected use, so it’s *possible* to escape and
inject something unintended. However, such abuse is unsupported and will not
be considered when making changes to the templates.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AutoCfg](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)
- Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg`output in build scripts.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A common error type for the `autocfg`crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit](https://docs.rs/fn.emit.html)
- Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)- possibility
- Indicates to rustc that a config flag should not generate an `unexpected_cfgs`warning
- [new](https://docs.rs/fn.new.html)
- Creates a new `AutoCfg`instance.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_env.html)- env
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var`changes.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_path.html)- path
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if `path`changes.

[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// Creates a new `AutoCfg` instance.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    ///
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// # Common errors
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// - `rustc` can't be executed, from `RUSTC` or in the `PATH`.
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// - The version output from `rustc` can't be parsed.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// - `OUT_DIR` is not set in the environment, or is not a writable directory.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    ///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    pub fn new() -> Result<Self, Error> {
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        match env::var_os("OUT_DIR") {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            Some(d) => Self::with_dir(d),
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            None => Err(error::from_str("no OUT_DIR specified!")),
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// Creates a new `AutoCfg` instance with the specified output directory.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    ///
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// # Common errors
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    ///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// - `rustc` can't be executed, from `RUSTC` or in the `PATH`.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// - The version output from `rustc` can't be parsed.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// - `dir` is not a writable directory.
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    ///
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    pub fn with_dir<T: Into<PathBuf>>(dir: T) -> Result<Self, Error> {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        let rustc = Rustc::new();
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        let rustc_version = try!(rustc.version());
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        let target = env::var_os("TARGET");
[192](https://docs.rs#192)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        // Sanity check the output directory
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        let dir = dir.into();
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        let meta = try!(fs::metadata(&dir).map_err(error::from_io));
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        if !meta.is_dir() || meta.permissions().readonly() {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)            return Err(error::from_str("output path is not a writable directory"));
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        }
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        let mut ac = AutoCfg {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            rustflags: rustflags(&target, &dir),
[202](https://docs.rs#202)            out_dir: dir,
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            rustc: rustc,
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            rustc_version: rustc_version,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            target: target,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            no_std: false,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)            edition: None,
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            uuid: new_uuid(),
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        };
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        // Sanity check with and without `std`.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        if ac.probe_raw("").is_err() {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)            if ac.probe_raw("#![no_std]").is_ok() {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)                ac.no_std = true;
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            } else {
[216](https://docs.rs#216)                // Neither worked, so assume nothing...
[217](https://docs.rs#217)                let warning = b"warning: autocfg could not probe for `std`\n";
[218](https://docs.rs#218)                stderr().write_all(warning).ok();
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        Ok(ac)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Returns whether `AutoCfg` is using `#![no_std]` in its probes.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// This is automatically detected during construction -- if an empty probe
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// fails while one with `#![no_std]` succeeds, then the attribute will be
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// used for all further probes. This is usually only necessary when the
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// `TARGET` lacks `std` altogether. If neither succeeds, `no_std` is not
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// set, but that `AutoCfg` will probably only work for version checks.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// This attribute changes the implicit [prelude] from `std` to `core`,
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// which may affect the paths you need to use in other probes. It also
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// restricts some types that otherwise get additional methods in `std`,
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// like floating-point trigonometry and slice sorting.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    ///
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// See also [`set_no_std`](#method.set_no_std).
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    ///
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    /// [prelude]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/preludes.html#the-no_std-attribute
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    pub fn no_std(&self) -> bool {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        self.no_std
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)

[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// See also [`no_std`](#method.no_std).
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    pub fn set_no_std(&mut self, no_std: bool) {

[249](https://docs.rs#249)    }
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// Returns the `--edition` string that is currently being passed to `rustc`, if any,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// as configured by the [`set_edition`][Self::set_edition] method.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    pub fn edition(&self) -> Option<&str> {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        match self.edition {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            Some(ref edition) => Some(&**edition),
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            None => None,
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        }
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    }
[259](https://docs.rs#259)
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// Sets the `--edition` string that will be passed to `rustc`,
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// or `None` to leave the compiler at its default edition.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    ///
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// See also [The Rust Edition Guide](https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/).
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// **Warning:** Setting an unsupported edition will likely cause **all** subsequent probes to
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// fail! As of this writing, the known editions and their minimum Rust versions are:
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    ///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    /// | Edition | Version    |
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// | ------- | ---------- |
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// | 2015    | 1.27.0[^1] |
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// | 2018    | 1.31.0     |
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// | 2021    | 1.56.0     |
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// | 2024    | 1.85.0     |
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    ///
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// [^1]: Prior to 1.27.0, Rust was effectively 2015 Edition by default, but the concept hadn't
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// been established yet, so the explicit `--edition` flag wasn't supported either.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    pub fn set_edition(&mut self, edition: Option<String>) {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        self.edition = edition;
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    }
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// Tests whether the current `rustc` reports a version greater than
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// or equal to "`major`.`minor`".
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    pub fn probe_rustc_version(&self, major: usize, minor: usize) -> bool {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        self.rustc_version >= Version::new(major, minor, 0)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    }
[286](https://docs.rs#286)
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// Sets a `cfg` value of the form `rustc_major_minor`, like `rustc_1_29`,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// if the current `rustc` is at least that version.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn emit_rustc_version(&self, major: usize, minor: usize) {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        let cfg_flag = format!("rustc_{}_{}", major, minor);
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        emit_possibility(&cfg_flag);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        if self.probe_rustc_version(major, minor) {
[293](https://docs.rs#293)            emit(&cfg_flag);
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        }
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    }
[296](https://docs.rs#296)
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// Returns a new (hopefully unique) crate name for probes.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    fn new_crate_name(&self) -> String {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        #[allow(deprecated)]
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        static ID: AtomicUsize = ATOMIC_USIZE_INIT;
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        let id = ID.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        format!("autocfg_{:016x}_{}", self.uuid, id)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    fn probe_fmt<'a>(&self, source: Arguments<'a>) -> Result<(), Error> {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        let crate_name = self.new_crate_name();
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        let mut command = self.rustc.command();
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        command
[310](https://docs.rs#310)            .arg("--crate-name")
[311](https://docs.rs#311)            .arg(&crate_name)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            .arg("--crate-type=lib")
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            .arg("--out-dir")
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            .arg(&self.out_dir)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            .arg("--emit=llvm-ir");
[316](https://docs.rs#316)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        if let Some(edition) = self.edition.as_ref() {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)            command.arg("--edition").arg(edition);
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        }
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        if let Some(target) = self.target.as_ref() {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            command.arg("--target").arg(target);
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        command.args(&self.rustflags);
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        command.arg("-").stdin(Stdio::piped());
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        let mut child = try!(command.spawn().map_err(error::from_io));
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        let mut stdin = child.stdin.take().expect("rustc stdin");
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        try!(stdin.write_fmt(source).map_err(error::from_io));
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        drop(stdin);
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        match child.wait() {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            Ok(status) if status.success() => {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                // Try to remove the output file so it doesn't look like a build product for
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                // systems like bazel -- but this is best-effort, so we can ignore failure.
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                // The probe itself is already considered successful at this point.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                let mut file = self.out_dir.join(crate_name);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                file.set_extension("ll");
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                let _ = fs::remove_file(file);
[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                Ok(())
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            }
[345](https://docs.rs#345)            Ok(status) => Err(error::from_exit(status)),
[346](https://docs.rs#346)            Err(error) => Err(error::from_io(error)),
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    fn probe<'a>(&self, code: Arguments<'a>) -> bool {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        let result = if self.no_std {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            self.probe_fmt(format_args!("#![no_std]\n{}", code))
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        } else {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            self.probe_fmt(code)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        };
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        result.is_ok()
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    }
[358](https://docs.rs#358)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// Tests whether the given code can be compiled as a Rust library.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    ///
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// This will only return `Ok` if the compiler ran and exited successfully,
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// per `ExitStatus::success()`.
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// The code is passed to the compiler exactly as-is, notably not even
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// adding the [`#![no_std]`][Self::no_std] attribute like other probes.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// Raw probes are useful for testing functionality that's not yet covered
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// by the rest of the `AutoCfg` API. For example, the following attribute
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// **must** be used at the crate level, so it wouldn't work within the code
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// templates used by other `probe_*` methods.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// ```
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// # extern crate autocfg;
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// # // Normally, cargo will set `OUT_DIR` for build scripts.
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// # let exe = std::env::current_exe().unwrap();
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// # std::env::set_var("OUT_DIR", exe.parent().unwrap());
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// let ac = autocfg::new();
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// assert!(ac.probe_raw("#![no_builtins]").is_ok());
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// ```
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    ///
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// Rust nightly features could be tested as well -- ideally including a
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// code sample to ensure the unstable feature still works as expected.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// For example, `slice::group_by` was renamed to `chunk_by` when it was
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// stabilized, even though the feature name was unchanged, so testing the
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// `#![feature(..)]` alone wouldn't reveal that. For larger snippets,
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// [`include_str!`] may be useful to load them from separate files.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// ```
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// # extern crate autocfg;
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// # // Normally, cargo will set `OUT_DIR` for build scripts.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// # let exe = std::env::current_exe().unwrap();
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// # std::env::set_var("OUT_DIR", exe.parent().unwrap());
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// let ac = autocfg::new();
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// let code = r#"
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     #![feature(slice_group_by)]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///     pub fn probe(slice: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[i32]> {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    ///         slice.group_by(|a, b| a == b)
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///     }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// "#;
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// if ac.probe_raw(code).is_ok() {
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///     autocfg::emit("has_slice_group_by");
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// }
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// ```
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    pub fn probe_raw(&self, code: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        self.probe_fmt(format_args!("{}", code))
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    }

[546](https://docs.rs#546)}
[547](https://docs.rs#547)
[548](https://docs.rs#548)fn mangle(s: &str) -> String {
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    s.chars()
[550](https://docs.rs#550)        .map(|c| match c {
[551](https://docs.rs#551)            'A'...'Z' | 'a'...'z' | '0'...'9' => c,
[552](https://docs.rs#552)            _ => '_',
[553](https://docs.rs#553)        })
[554](https://docs.rs#554)        .collect()
[555](https://docs.rs#555)}
[556](https://docs.rs#556)
[557](https://docs.rs#557)fn dir_contains_target(
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    target: &Option<OsString>,
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    dir: &Path,
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    cargo_target_dir: Option<OsString>,
[561](https://docs.rs#561)) -> bool {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    target
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        .as_ref()
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        .and_then(|target| {
[565](https://docs.rs#565)            dir.to_str().and_then(|dir| {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)                let mut cargo_target_dir = cargo_target_dir
[567](https://docs.rs#567)                    .map(PathBuf::from)
[568](https://docs.rs#568)                    .unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from("target"));
[569](https://docs.rs#569)                cargo_target_dir.push(target);
[570](https://docs.rs#570)
[571](https://docs.rs#571)                cargo_target_dir
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                    .to_str()
[573](https://docs.rs#573)                    .map(|cargo_target_dir| dir.contains(cargo_target_dir))
[574](https://docs.rs#574)            })
[575](https://docs.rs#575)        })
[576](https://docs.rs#576)        .unwrap_or(false)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)}
[578](https://docs.rs#578)
[579](https://docs.rs#579)fn rustflags(target: &Option<OsString>, dir: &Path) -> Vec<String> {
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    // Starting with rust-lang/cargo#9601, shipped in Rust 1.55, Cargo always sets
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    // CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS for any host/target build script invocation. This
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    // includes any source of flags, whether from the environment, toml config, or
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    // whatever may come in the future. The value is either an empty string, or a
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    // list of arguments separated by the ASCII unit separator (US), 0x1f.
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    if let Ok(a) = env::var("CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS") {
[586](https://docs.rs#586)        return if a.is_empty() {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)            Vec::new()
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        } else {
[589](https://docs.rs#589)            a.split('\x1f').map(str::to_string).collect()
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        };
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    }
[592](https://docs.rs#592)
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    // Otherwise, we have to take a more heuristic approach, and we don't
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    // support values from toml config at all.
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    //
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    // Cargo only applies RUSTFLAGS for building TARGET artifact in
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    // cross-compilation environment. Sadly, we don't have a way to detect
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    // when we're building HOST artifact in a cross-compilation environment,
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    // so for now we only apply RUSTFLAGS when cross-compiling an artifact.
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    //
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    // See https://github.com/cuviper/autocfg/pull/10#issuecomment-527575030.

# AutoCfg in autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autocfg/1.5.1/autocfg/struct.AutoCfg.html

`pub struct AutoCfg { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg` output in build scripts.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `AutoCfg` instance.

[§](https://docs.rs#common-errors)Common errors

- `rustc`can’t be executed, from- `RUSTC`or in the- `PATH`.
- The version output from `rustc`can’t be parsed.
- `OUT_DIR`is not set in the environment, or is not a writable directory.

Creates a new `AutoCfg` instance with the specified output directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#common-errors-1)Common errors

- `rustc`can’t be executed, from- `RUSTC`or in the- `PATH`.
- The version output from `rustc`can’t be parsed.
- `dir`is not a writable directory.

3fn main() {
4    // Normally, cargo will set `OUT_DIR` for build scripts.
5    let ac = autocfg::AutoCfg::with_dir("target").unwrap();
6
7    // When this feature was stabilized, it also renamed the method to
8    // `chunk_by`, so it's important to *use* the feature in your probe.
9    let code = r#"
10        #![feature(slice_group_by)]
11        pub fn probe(slice: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[i32]> {
12            slice.group_by(|a, b| a == b)
13        }
14    "#;
15    if ac.probe_raw(code).is_ok() {
16        autocfg::emit("has_slice_group_by");
17    }
18}

Returns whether `AutoCfg` is using `#![no_std]` in its probes.

This is automatically detected during construction – if an empty probe
fails while one with `#![no_std]` succeeds, then the attribute will be
used for all further probes. This is usually only necessary when the
`TARGET` lacks `std` altogether. If neither succeeds, `no_std` is not
set, but that `AutoCfg` will probably only work for version checks.

This attribute changes the implicit [prelude](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/preludes.html#the-no_std-attribute) from `std` to `core`,
which may affect the paths you need to use in other probes. It also
restricts some types that otherwise get additional methods in `std`,
like floating-point trigonometry and slice sorting.

See also [ set_no_std](https://docs.rs#method.set_no_std).

Sets a `cfg` value of the form `rustc_major_minor`, like `rustc_1_29`,
if the current `rustc` is at least that version.

Tests whether the given code can be compiled as a Rust library.

This will only return `Ok` if the compiler ran and exited successfully,
per `ExitStatus::success()`.
The code is passed to the compiler exactly as-is, notably not even
adding the [ #![no_std]](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html#method.no_std) attribute like other probes.

Raw probes are useful for testing functionality that’s not yet covered
by the rest of the `AutoCfg` API. For example, the following attribute
**must** be used at the crate level, so it wouldn’t work within the code
templates used by other `probe_*` methods.

```
let ac = autocfg::new();
assert!(ac.probe_raw("#![no_builtins]").is_ok());
```
Rust nightly features could be tested as well – ideally including a
code sample to ensure the unstable feature still works as expected.
For example, `slice::group_by` was renamed to `chunk_by` when it was
stabilized, even though the feature name was unchanged, so testing the
`#![feature(..)]` alone wouldn’t reveal that. For larger snippets,
[ include_str!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.include_str.html) may be useful to load them from separate files.

```
let ac = autocfg::new();
let code = r#"
    #![feature(slice_group_by)]
    pub fn probe(slice: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[i32]> {
        slice.group_by(|a, b| a == b)
    }
"#;
if ac.probe_raw(code).is_ok() {
    autocfg::emit("has_slice_group_by");
}
```

Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.

This looks like: `cargo:rustc-cfg=CFG`

Cargo will use this in arguments to rustc, like `--cfg CFG`.

This does not automatically call [ emit_possibility](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)
so the compiler my generate an

[. However, all the builtin emit methods on](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2024/05/06/check-cfg.html)

`unexpected_cfgs` warning[call](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)

`AutoCfg`[automatically.](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)

8    // `chunk_by`, so it's important to *use* the feature in your probe.

11        pub fn probe(slice: &[i32]) -> impl Iterator<Item = &[i32]> {
12            slice.group_by(|a, b| a == b)
13        }
14    "#;
15    if ac.probe_raw(code).is_ok() {
16        autocfg::emit("has_slice_group_by");
17    }
18}
```

# rerun_env in autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autocfg/1.5.1/autocfg/fn.rerun_env.html

`pub fn rerun_env(var: &`[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))## Expand description

Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var` changes.

This looks like: `cargo:rerun-if-env-changed=VAR`

This requires at least cargo 0.21.0, corresponding to rustc 1.20.0. Earlier versions of cargo will simply ignore the directive.

# autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autocfg/latest/target-redirect/autocfg/index.html

## Expand description

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[build-dependencies]
autocfg = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
fn main() {
    let ac = autocfg::new();
    ac.emit_has_type("i128");
    // (optional) We don't need to rerun for anything external.
    autocfg::rerun_path("build.rs");
}
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

[§](https://docs.rs#caution)Caution

Many of the probing methods of `AutoCfg` document the particular template they
use, **subject to change**. The inputs are not validated to make sure they are
semantically correct for their expected use, so it’s *possible* to escape and
inject something unintended. However, such abuse is unsupported and will not
be considered when making changes to the templates.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AutoCfg](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)
- Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg`output in build scripts.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A common error type for the `autocfg`crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit](https://docs.rs/fn.emit.html)
- Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)- possibility
- Indicates to rustc that a config flag should not generate an `unexpected_cfgs`warning
- [new](https://docs.rs/fn.new.html)
- Creates a new `AutoCfg`instance.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_env.html)- env
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var`changes.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_path.html)- path
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if `path`changes.
